latin: Quodcunque contingens deus sciuit esse futurum, necessario sciuit illud esse futurum.
translation: Whatever contingent thing God knew would be future, he knew necessarily that it would be future.
translator: original translation, drafted 2026-09-26 by WRITER-full-batch2, from Latin at farmer1998:11321

sources.text: Thomas Aquinas, Summa theologiae, 1, q. 14, a. 13
sources.pico_relation: Edelheit finds Thomas emphasizing the same necessity shortly after the passage behind thesis 2.4

doctrine: The thesis holds that whatever contingent future thing God knew, he knew it necessarily (farmer1998:11321). Edelheit states that thesis 5 holds that whatever future contingency God knows is known to him in a necessary fashion, and that this necessity is emphasized again by Thomas a little later in the same discussion as thesis 4, in the Summa, 1, q. 14, a. 13 (edelheit2022:10331). Farmer groups this thesis with 2.2-9 under the divine omnipotence/free will problem (farmer1998:11348).
historiography: Edelheit (2022) reads theses 4 and 5 as a pair restating, in Pico's compressed form, the same page of Thomas's Summa, 1, q. 14, a. 13 (edelheit2022:10331).

quotations.text: Thesis 5 states that, whatever future contingency God knows is known to Him in a necessary fashion.

not_established: Not established by the sources consulted.
